definition: Latent inhibition is slower learning about a stimulus because it has previously been experienced without any obvious consequence. In psychology, it reflects the tendency for familiar, previously irrelevant stimuli to attract less attention when they later become important for learning.

reasons: The first sentence is broadly supported, but the second sentence adds an interpretive claim about familiar, previously irrelevant stimuli attracting less attention when they later become important for learning; the packet instead says latent inhibition is a retardation in learning after prior exposure without explicit consequences and discusses attentional style in relation to reduced latent inhibition, not this exact formulation.

The definition’s second sentence claims that latent inhibition “reflects the tendency for familiar, previously irrelevant stimuli to attract less attention when they later become important for learning,” but the packet does not explicitly state this “less attention when later become important” phrasing. It discusses a “leaky” attentional style and difficulty inhibiting irrelevant information, plus associations with creativity/peripheral details, but not the specific general attention-to-importance mechanism described in the definition.
